lessons.title: Modelling Your Dilution From Angel Round to Series B

children.text: Every lesson in this chapter looked at one round in isolation. Founders do not live in one round. Meera started with 60% of TiffinBox and will finish this lesson with 17.11%, across four financing events spread over six years, none of which was unfair or unusual. The point of a dilution model is not to avoid that path. It is to see it in advance, so each decision is made with the last one in view.

body.text: Your percentage will fall at every round. What matters is whether it falls for a reason. A founder who has modelled three rounds ahead negotiates differently from one who models the round in front of them.

children.text: A dilution model is not complicated. It is one calculation repeated per round, and it needs four inputs each time. Get these right and the arithmetic takes care of itself.

body.caption: The inputs you need for each future round

cells: The size of the new investor's slice
Raising less than the plan needs, then raising again sooner
The other half of the dilution ratio
Assuming a step-up that the business will not have earned
How much is carved out before the round, usually from you
Leaving it out of the model entirely
Extra shares created just before the round
Using an old estimate instead of the contractual conversion

content.caption: One formula, applied once per round, with the previous round's output as the next round's input

children.text: Series A: existing non-pool shares are 10,000 founder shares plus 1,250 angel shares plus 5,000 seed shares, and the note converts into 584, giving 16,834. The investor takes 25% and the pool is reset to 15%, both pre-money, so this must fit into 60%. Total = 16,834 ÷ 0.60 = 28,057 shares. Pool = 4,209 options, investor = 7,014 shares, and Meera is 6,000 ÷ 28,057 = 21.39%.

Series B: existing non-pool shares are now 28,057 minus the 4,209-option pool, which is 23,848. The new investor takes 20% and the pool is reset to 12%, so this fits into 68%. Total = 23,848 ÷ 0.68 = 35,071 shares. Investor = 7,014 shares, pool = 4,209, and Meera is 6,000 ÷ 35,071 = 17.11%.

Note on consistency: this model uses the note's contractual conversion of 584 shares from the previous lesson, not the 500-share estimate the old cap table carried. Percentages here therefore differ slightly from the earlier illustrations, which is exactly what happens in real life when an assumption is replaced by a contract.

body.title: Who owns TiffinBox at each stage (% fully diluted)

children.text: The two lines cross between the seed and Series A rounds. That crossing point is worth understanding before it arrives, because it is where a founding team stops being the majority owner of its own company. It is not a disaster, and Chapter 4 explains why control does not move on the same day the percentage does, but it should never be a surprise.
The Percentage Fell. The Money Did Not.
Meera's 6,000 shares never changed. Her percentage fell by roughly two thirds. Now put the price per share next to it, because ownership percentage is only half of a founder's outcome.

stats.context: A modest round after a pool reset and a note conversion

body.text: Look at the Series A row. The price per share barely moved above the seed price, even though the company raised ₹6.25 crore at a ₹25 crore post-money valuation. The reason is that the pool was reset to 15% and the note converted at its cap, both of which added shares to the pre-money count. Valuation went up. Price per share almost did not. That gap is where founder value quietly leaks, and it only shows up in a model that includes the pool and the convertibles.

A model that omits the pool top-up and the convertibles is not conservative, it is wrong. In this journey those two items moved the founders' Series A stake by several percentage points on their own. Build the model with them included, then build a second version with a larger pool and a lower valuation, because that is the version you may actually have to live with.

body.title: Model the Series B
body.prompt: After the Series A, TiffinBox has 28,057 fully diluted shares, of which 4,209 are the ESOP pool. The Series B investor will take 20% and the pool will be reset to 12% of the post-round capital, both before the round. How many fully diluted shares will exist after the Series B? Round to the nearest whole share.
body.explanation: Existing non-pool shares are 28,057 minus 4,209 = 23,848, and they must fit into 100% minus 20% minus 12% = 68%. 23,848 ÷ 0.68 = 35,070.6, so about 35,071 shares. The investor receives 7,014 shares and the pool becomes 4,209 options.

body.title: Name the basis
body.textWithBlank: A dilution model is only meaningful if every round is calculated on a fully ___ basis, including the option pool and every convertible instrument.
body.explanation: Modelling on an issued basis flatters every number, because it leaves out the pool and the convertibles, which are exactly the items that cost founders the most.

body.title: Which assumption hurts most?
body.question: You are modelling a Series A two years out. Changing which single assumption is most likely to move your final ownership by several percentage points?
options: Whether the round closes in March or in June
Whether the investor takes a board seat
Whether the required ESOP pool is 10% or 18%, created pre-money
Whether the investment is paid in one tranche or two
body.explanation: A pre-money pool is paid for entirely by the existing shareholders, so the difference between a 10% and an 18% pool moves founder ownership by several points. Timing, board seats and tranching matter for other reasons, but they do not change the share count the way a pool reset does.

body.title: Modelling backwards from where you want to end
body.scenario: You are a solo founder of a Jaipur B2B startup holding 62% fully diluted after your seed round, with 24,000 fully diluted shares including a 3,000-option pool. You expect to raise a Series A and then a Series B before any exit, and you have decided you want to still hold at least 30% after the Series B. Your lead investor's standard terms are a 20% to 25% stake plus a pool reset to 15%, pre-money, at each round.
body.prompt: Model whether 30% is achievable, and list the levers you would use.
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the arithmetic on the investor's standard terms.
Series A: existing non-pool shares are 24,000 minus 3,000 = 21,000, fitting into 100% minus 25% minus 15% = 60%. Total = 21,000 ÷ 0.60 = 35,000 shares, pool = 5,250, investor = 8,750. Your shares are 62% of 24,000, which is 14,880, so you hold 14,880 ÷ 35,000 = 42.51%.
Series B on the same terms: existing non-pool shares are 35,000 minus 5,250 = 29,750, fitting into 60% again. Total = 29,750 ÷ 0.60 = 49,583 shares. You hold 14,880 ÷ 49,583 = 30.01%.

So 30% is just about achievable on standard terms, with no margin for error. Any one thing going worse, a larger pool, a bigger investor stake, or a convertible you forgot, puts you below it.

The levers, in order of impact:
1. Pool size and timing. Getting each pool reset sized to a real hiring plan, or split between pre-money and post-money, is worth more than any other single change.
2. Investor percentage. The difference between 20% and 25% at two rounds compounds. Raising at a proportionally higher valuation for the same cheque gets you there.
3. Skip or shrink a round. If the Series A can carry you to profitability, a smaller Series B, or none at all, protects more ownership than any clause.
4. Count what already exists. Unallocated options from the previous pool should count towards the next reset rather than sitting on top of it.
5. Secondary instead of primary. If you need personal liquidity, selling a small number of shares at the Series B, covered in Chapter 4, is different from issuing new ones.

The discipline: decide the number you want to protect, model backwards from it, and treat every term sheet as an input to that model rather than a standalone event.

body.title: Building your own dilution model
steps: Start with today's fully diluted share count, split into non-pool shares and pool options.
List every outstanding convertible with its cap and discount, and add the shares it would produce at your expected next-round price.
For each future round, write down four assumptions: money raised, post-money valuation, investor percentage and required pool.
Apply the formula once per round, using each round's output as the next round's input.
Track your own share count separately, since it does not change, and divide it by each round's total.
Add a price-per-share column so you can see value alongside percentage.
Build a pessimistic version with larger pools and lower valuations, and check you can live with it.
Re-run the whole model every time a term sheet arrives, before you respond to it.

body.title: Two ways to read the same model

columns.label: Percentage thinking
points: Focuses on how much of the company you keep
Drives negotiation on pool size, valuation and round size
Matters for control thresholds and board composition
Can push founders into under-raising to protect a number

columns.label: Value thinking
points: Focuses on what your shares are worth at each price
Accepts dilution when it buys a larger, more valuable company
Matters for exit proceeds and personal liquidity
Can push founders into over-raising at valuations they cannot grow into

body.label: The founder's real question
body.value: Is the slice smaller than the pie is bigger?
body.context: Meera gave up about two thirds of her percentage across four rounds and ended with shares worth roughly 5,700 times their starting value. Dilution is only expensive when the money raised does not build more value than the ownership it costs.

cards.definition: A round-by-round projection of fully diluted ownership, built from assumptions about money raised, valuation, pool size and convertibles.
The increase in price per share or valuation from one round to the next.
An increase in the option pool to an agreed percentage of post-round capital, usually required before each new round.
All fully diluted shares other than the option pool. The base the model squeezes into whatever percentage is left.
Share count multiplied by the latest round price. Real only when someone actually buys at that price.
The round at which investors together pass the founders in fully diluted ownership.

points: A dilution model is one formula applied once per round, with each round's output feeding the next.
Every round needs four assumptions: money raised, post-money valuation, investor percentage and required pool.
Across four financing events, Meera went from 60.00% to 17.11% and the founders together from 100% to 28.51%.
Investors passed the founders in combined ownership between the seed and Series A rounds, which is normal and should never be a surprise.
Her share count never changed, and the paper value of those shares rose roughly 5,700 times.
A valuation increase can be swallowed by a pool reset and a converting note, so the price per share barely moves. Only a full model shows this.
Model a pessimistic case with bigger pools and lower valuations, and re-run the whole model before responding to any term sheet.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other startups and people described are fictional, and all valuations, prices, share counts and percentages are illustrative rather than benchmarks. Share counts are rounded to whole shares, so percentages may differ slightly in the second decimal place, and columns may total 100.01%. Real rounds involve pricing, valuation and regulatory requirements that depend on the investor and the structure. Consult a qualified chartered accountant, company secretary or lawyer before acting on any model.
